item.title: ‘COVID 2.0’: Lawmakers push back on sweeping health 'police power' in key battleground state
item.description: Pennsylvania lawmakers told Fox News Digital the state's 502-page health code rewrite amounts to government overreach worse than COVID-era lockdowns.
item.content:encoded:
Pennsylvania lawmakers are warning that proposed changes to the state’s public health rules could usher in "COVID 2.0," giving health officials sweeping "police power" over residents during future disease outbreaks.

Lawmakers opposing Pennsylvania's planned 502-page rewrite of state health code rules are urging the public to submit comments before the deadline, warning the proposal could serve as a roadmap to unfettered and intrusive restrictions and surveillance efforts, including the reported ability for agency representatives to enter private homes.

"This absolutely is COVID 2.0, but it's even worse because [Governor] Josh Shapiro is trying to circumnavigate or skirt the constitutional provision that we the people in Pennsylvania voted to take that kind of power away from the governor," said state Rep. Russ Diamond, R-Lebanon, who is leading the charge against the policy changes.

"We were the only state in the nation to reduce our governor's powers by a constitutional amendment after COVID," Diamond said, adding that "surveillance, segregation and quarantine" are areas being assessed.

SOVIET-BORN ANALYST EXPOSES HOW PANDEMIC-ERA NEIGHBOR SNITCHING UNLOCKED A 'NATURE OF EVIL' IN AMERICA

Pennsylvania voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2021 limiting the duration of a governor’s disaster declaration to 21 days unless extended by the General Assembly. Those emergency powers played a central role in then-Gov. Tom Wolf’s statewide mitigation orders.

In the 502-page proposed Regulation 10-242, Communicable and Noncommunicable Diseases, the Pennsylvania Department of Health proposes expanding the list of reportable diseases, infections and conditions and updating the rules to reflect changing expert standards. "The Department proposes to add language in this subsection, indicating that the Department or a local health authority may enter an apartment, a building, a health care facility, a school, college or university, or other location as necessary to conduct its investigation under 208 this chapter," one provision highlighted by critics reads.

"I don't think that we want a very left-leaning governor with his Department of Health and their henchmen having this kind of police power in Pennsylvania," Diamond said.

A spokesperson for Health Secretary Dr. Debra Bogen — who led the Pittsburgh area’s COVID mitigation response — said Shapiro "did not personally propose" the updates and rejected critics’ characterizations.

"Any misconstruing of these proposed changes designed to scare Pennsylvanians is inaccurate and disingenuous," Neil Ruhland told Fox News Digital.

A Shapiro spokesperson also responded to criticism Wednesday, saying the governor’s philosophy is that "public health depends on trust" and emphasizing that the proposed health regulations are part of a larger effort to update about 200 regulatory areas across state agencies.

Lapowsky told Fox News Digital that the public, stakeholders, independent regulators and the legislature can review and respond to the proposed changes.

"Once public comment concludes later this month, [Shapiro] will weigh in, and the regulations will be revised accordingly," she said.

Lapowsky said Shapiro’s emphasis on public trust includes respecting parental rights. Critics say the proposed regulations could give health officials greater authority over certain disease-control measures involving children, including masking. Lapowsky added that the governor believes "government should work closely with the people it serves."

GOV SHAPIRO SUES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OVER ‘LIFESAVING REPRODUCTIVE CARE’ IN ESCALATING ABORTION BATTLE

Ruhland said the Pennsylvania Department of Health began analyzing and proposing regulatory updates several years ago and that the regulations in question are 25 years old and need modernization to "better support evolving public health needs and manage dangerous disease."

While the proposed regulations do not themselves enact a new mask mandate, they would broaden disease-control language beyond "surveillance," a term central to litigation over Pennsylvania’s statewide school masking order during the pandemic.

Pennsylvania House Minority Leader Jesse Topper told Fox News Digital that although the proposed regulations directly affect Pennsylvania, Americans elsewhere should also pay attention.

"Everybody in the United States was impacted by COVID one way or another," said Topper, R-McConnellsburg.

"We were one of the worst locked-down states in the entire nation. And we had one of the worst death rates from COVID… We don't want unelected bureaucrats making those decisions. We need to follow the [Commonwealth] Constitution, which says, ‘Hey, you can declare a public health disaster emergency if you want. But after 21 days, the legislature gets to say whether you can continue that or not’."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

State Sen. Doug Mastriano, R-Gettysburg, who, along with Diamond, led demonstrations against lockdown policies during COVID, told Fox News Digital that the proposed regulations are an "end-round" around voters.

"Pennsylvania endured enough government overreach during COVID. We will not go back," said Mastriano, whom President Donald Trump nominated to serve as U.S. ambassador to Slovakia.

Jason Richey, an attorney and the Republican nominee for lieutenant governor, also dubbed the changes "COVID 2.0."

"These are even worse than the COVID rules... [DOH] can look at your medical records. They can enter any building and go in without a warrant to do an investigation. They can even take your kid from school and talk to him privately without your consent," Richey said in a video recorded outside a Pennsylvania Department of Health office in Lehigh County last week.

Beyond the public health implications, Topper said he is concerned that the proposed regulations would expand government authority.

Topper and Ruhland both encouraged Pennsylvanians to submit feedback on the proposed regulations before Monday’s public-comment deadline.

item.title: 'Leftist delusions' face reckoning as one of America's biggest colleges makes major shake-up
item.description: UT Austin drops women's studies, gender studies and ethnic studies majors amid low enrollment and political pressure from Texas state leaders.
item.content:encoded:
Texas’ flagship public university is ending new enrollment in three majors focused on gender, sexuality and race in a move that is being hailed by many conservatives as a major victory.

Students applying to the University of Texas at Austin can no longer select Women’s and Gender Studies, Mexican American and Latina/o Studies or African and African Diaspora Studies as majors, the institution has confirmed to Fox News Digital. The move follows a slew of other universities dropping similar majors and heated internal deliberations at UT Austin about whether to keep theirs.

"In recognition of the changing degree offerings in the Department of Social and Cultural Analysis, the University is no longer enrolling new students in three majors: Mexican American and Latina/o Studies, African and African Diaspora Studies, and Women’s & Gender Studies," a university spokesman told Fox News Digital.

"So, as you might expect, those majors have been removed from the University’s admissions applications to avoid new students enrolling in majors that are changing. Students currently enrolled in those majors will be able to complete their degree," the statement continued. 

LIBERAL FACULTY STILL HUGELY OUTNUMBER CONSERVATIVES IN HIGHER EDUCATION: REPORT

"I don’t know the particulars of UT Austin’s programs. But this news is unsurprising. Across the Anglosphere, ethnic and sexuality studies have long been captured by political activists," Timur Kuran, a professor of economics and political science at Duke University, wrote on X. "Other state universities, and even private ones, will follow."

Low enrollment has been part of the broader debate over the programs, although UT Austin has not publicly said it was the reason for ending new enrollment in the three majors.

Earlier this year, the Austin American-Statesman reported that the university had just 307 students enrolled across the entirety of African and African diaspora studies, Mexican American and Latino studies, women and gender studies and American studies, citing institutional data. That represents less than 1% of the 44,315 undergraduates who were enrolled at the university in fall 2025.

UT Austin, which is one of the largest universities in the nation, has also faced growing pressure from Republican state and federal officials over how it handles race, gender and other politically sensitive subjects. The University of Texas System has reviewed courses on gender identity to assess compliance with state and federal law and alignment with Board of Regents priorities.

An internal email obtained by the Austin American-Statesman indicates that, while the majors may be on the way out, much of the coursework could remain. The plan appears to be to consolidate the defunct majors into a single offering.

JUSTICE DEPARTMENT LAUNCHES TITLE VI INVESTIGATION INTO DEI PROGRAMS AT ARIZONA STATE UNIVERSITY

"Gender and ethnic studies have transformed the study of the humanities and social sciences, and now they are what they are," Lisa Moore, the university’s chair of women and gender studies, said prior to the consolidation announcement. "We can’t unknow what we know… It’s just not the case that we can believe that only a small slice of human beings are responsible for everything that’s good about the world."

Conservatives, unsurprisingly, have a less rosy view of the field.

Steve McGuire, a fellow at the American Council of Trustees and Alumni, called axing the majors "the pedagogically responsible thing to do."

"Excellent news. These programs are not ‘viewpoint diversity.’ They are ridiculous Leftist delusion[s] that have no place in truth-seeking institutions," J.D. Haltigan, a research fellow at the Centre for Heterodox Social Science, wrote on X. "They should be abolished entirely from every institution of higher-learning."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS

Some on the right see this as a sign of things to come.

"Every red state should follow suit with their universities," independent scholar Varad Mehta wrote on X.

Indeed, a number of universities in red states have already scaled back similar programs. Texas A&M University, Wichita State University, the University of Iowa and the University of Toledo are among the institutions to make such cuts.

UT Austin did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Friday.

item.title: China firm gave Iran lifeline to collect Hormuz tolls before pulling plug amid US warning
item.description: After briefly issuing a web security certificate for a portal linked to Iran's U.S.-sanctioned Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a Shanghai-based firm revoked it, though the move could still draw scrutiny under U.S. sanctions rules
item.content:encoded:
Iran’s sanctioned Persian Gulf Straits Authority (PGSA) regained secure online access for four days after a Shanghai-based internet security firm provided and then revoked its web credentials, enabling Tehran to vet vessels, collect Strait of Hormuz tolls and operate despite U.S. digital restrictions, global internet monitors said.

TrustAsia issued an automated domain-validated certificate, a routine process that verifies control of a website domain through server checks and typically does not involve manual vetting or background checks.

The move prompted U.S. sanctions experts, including Jeremy Paner, a partner at Hughes Hubbard & Reed, to urge TrustAsia to review its compliance program before offering further services to the IRGC-linked maritime authority — with Paner warning them to act "before it is too late."

The PGSA first said its website was disrupted Aug. 10 because of "the enemy's political influence on the internet service provision systems," according to a post on X.

IRAN REQUESTS TALKS WITH US AS WHITE HOUSE WARNS 'VIOLENCE WILL BE MET WITH VIOLENCE'

NetBlocks CEO Alp Toker told Fox News Digital that the authority had lost its web security credentials after the entity was added to the U.S. Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) sanctions list on May 27.

The loss of standard SSL/TLS certificates, Toker said, made the PGSA website inaccessible using standard browsers. This forced shipping firms to use unencrypted connections that, according to Toker, could leave their data vulnerable to interception.

While no data breaches resulting from the use of these connections have been made known, and there are no known instances in which a shipping firm’s data was intercepted and used to its detriment because of the certificate expiration, Toker said the site’s inaccessibility resulted in a shift to what he described as "insecure protocols."

"The digital transparency records are authoritative on this," he said, adding that the measure forced the traffic into a format that could be readily intercepted.

"This is a class of vulnerability open to government exploitation, rather than a corporate breach or personal data leak."

Toker claimed this could make it easier for authorities to read communications sent through the platform, potentially identifying shipping firms collaborating with the PGSA.

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

"The net result was that the website was more difficult to access, because most web browsers strongly encourage the use of secure HTTPS," Toker said, adding that any form submissions could have been easily "eavesdropped on because they're no longer encrypted in transit."

"The mentioned issue has been resolved, and the secure domain https://pgsa.ir is now once again available for submitting requests using any browser," the PGSA said six days later on Aug. 17 and in another post shared on X.

"If the issue recurs in the future, the HTTP domain will again be temporarily available using the Firefox browser."

Toker confirmed that Iran had turned to Shanghai-based certificate authority TrustAsia Technologies, which he said issued new digital security credentials to the PGSA despite the U.S. sanctions, restoring secure access to its website. 

"Iran’s IRGC extorts vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz through the so-called Persian Gulf Strait Authority," the Treasury Department said in May when designating the entity, adding that the PGSA "spearheads an Iranian-controlled scheme that flagrantly violates international law and U.S. sanctions."

"Anyone cooperating with the so-called strait authority may be providing support to and receiving services from the IRGC, which ultimately benefits from this attempted extortion, and may therefore be exposed to sanctions risk," the Treasury Department warned.

The Chinese firm bills itself as a "leading and professionally certified certification authority in China with its focus on trusted, secure and cryptographic communications in the digital world."

Its mission, it says, is to "Build trust everywhere in the digital world."

"Almost all of these root authorities do business with the U.S., so they tend to comply with U.S. sanctions," Toker said.

But TrustAsia, he noted, had "gone its own way, building a China-first certificate infrastructure that sidesteps the West."

Toker said TrustAsia had "simply gone ahead and issued Iran's PGSA with a new certificate, and Iran was once again collecting revenue from ships passing the Strait via its secure online portal."

TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS

Paner warned that U.S. authorities would have enforcement powers over such actions.

"The U.S. has incredibly broad authority to impose sanctions on non-Iranian companies that provide any sorts of services to sanctioned Iranian companies," he told Fox News Digital.

"Many times, that authority will be abbreviated or explained as being providers of material support to sanctioned Iranian companies. But in fact, any level of services whatsoever could be the basis for the United States imposing sanctions against the company for providing services to Iran."

"Restoration of the certificate is unequivocally sanctionable," Paner warned.

"Restoring the certificate is/was a service provided to the PGSA, which can be the basis for imposing sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13224, as amended.

"That authority does not in any way require that the service be ‘knowingly’ provided to the PGSA. In other words, the automated nature of the service is irrelevant and does not make the service any less sanctionable," the lawyer added.

In a statement to Fox News Digital on Aug. 20, a spokesperson for TrustAsia confirmed that the firm issued a "Domain Validated TLS certificate for pgsa.ir."

"Thank you for bringing this matter to our attention," the firm said before clarifying that "DV certificates are issued through automated validation of control over the requested domain names."

IRAN ACCELERATES EXECUTION CAMPAIGN AGAINST ANTI-REGIME ACTIVISTS AMID INTERNET CENSORSHIP

"This process does not verify or assert the legal identity, affiliation, or sanctions status of the entity operating or benefiting from the domain.

"As a result, the relationship described in your inquiry was not identified during the automated issuance process." Following the firm's review, TrustAsia said it "added the entire pgsa.ir domain namespace to our restricted-issuance list to prevent further issuance or renewal."

"We also expect to complete revocation of the existing certificate within this week," the spokesman said on Aug. 20.

These actions are precautionary compliance and risk-control measures. They should not be interpreted as a finding that the certificate was technically misissued, TrustAsia said.

Toker confirmed the TrustAsia certificate's privilege had been withdrawn on Aug. 21 at 12:15:25 UTC. "This usually means the issuer has taken action," he said.

The internet expert clarified that the revocation will gradually be coming into effect, with the firm "signaling that the PGSA certificate should no longer be trusted, and they're distributing this notice that privilege is withdrawn, usually meaning customer misuse or breached terms of use."

"The secure website will stop working in most browsers, unless the owners can find a certificate authority that's willing to issue a new certificate," Toker said.

IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY

After reviewing TrustAsia's statement, Paner also said that OFAC would expect the company to "use the discovery as an opportunity to enhance its compliance program before it is too late."

The former OFAC official clarified that Iran's revenue collection in the waterway would likely draw high-level scrutiny in Washington.

"Iran's attempt to extort the world in the movement of oil through the Strait of Hormuz is of the utmost importance to OFAC, which is the agency that implements and enforces U.S. economic sanctions."

Because major U.S. web browsers currently recognize TrustAsia’s root certificates, American systems would have automatically trusted the sanctioned Iranian portal.

Toker claimed the Treasury Department could have found TrustAsia in violation of sanctions for providing material assistance to a blocked entity, potentially forcing tech giants such as Google and Microsoft to revoke trust in TrustAsia.

There is no evidence that this process had begun or was likely to occur.

"This could have splintered the global chain of trust and potentially render much of the Chinese web inaccessible from the West," Toker warned.

IRAN IS NOT A NORMAL NATION YOU CAN MAKE DEALS WITH; IT’S A NATIONAL SECURITY THREAT

Paner clarified that the certificates authenticate the site, boosting its credibility, and suggested TrustAsia should have weighed the risks of working with sanctioned entities.

"There's always reputational risk involved in any company that decides to do business with the IRGC."

"If I were advising TrustAsia, I would at minimum immediately identify all other IRGC companies receiving services."

Paner added that this latest situation aligned with broader warnings from administration officials.

"I think this dovetails pretty nicely with Secretary Bessent's comments about how the coming sanctions are going to be unlike any that has come prior. Sanctions require a careful balancing of the costs and the benefits.

"When it's a Chinese tech company providing necessary services to the IRGC, I'm confident that the U.S. government is going to forego any sort of balancing in that regard."

The United States on Aug. 24 had sanctioned nearly 60 Iran-linked individuals, entities and vessels and expanded the threat of secondary sanctions, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. These did not include TrustAsia.

Bessent described the measures as part of an "economic onslaught" targeting Tehran’s global financial networks under "Operation Economic Outcast."

A Chinese Embassy spokesperson also said in a statement: "I am not aware of the specifics you mentioned. I have no information to provide."

Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the White House for comment.

item.title: Angel mom pleads with her party to 'grow up' on immigration after newlywed son killed in truck crash
item.description: Elizabeth Carter, a lifelong Democrat, says she is ashamed of her party after an illegal immigrant truck driver killed her newlywed son and his wife.
item.content:encoded:
A lifelong Democrat whose newlywed son and daughter-in-law were killed in a crash involving an illegal immigrant truck driver is pleading with her party to change course on immigration, saying she is "ashamed" of how her party has handled the issue.

"I was shocked and heartbroken to hear that the man responsible for our son and daughter-in-law's death, the driver of the 18-wheeler that they collided with, that he was a part of Biden's catch-and-release policy," angel mom Elizabeth Carter told "Hannity" Thursday.

Carter's son, William Micah "Billy" Carter, 25, and his wife, Jennifer Lynn Lower Carter, 24, were killed in November 2025, when their Subaru struck a tractor-trailer that had jackknifed across both lanes of U.S. Highway 20 in Oregon. The couple had been married for just 16 days.

WATCH: 'LIFELONG DEMOCRAT' ADMITS SHE IS ‘ASHAMED’ OF PARTY AFTER SON KILLED IN ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRASH

The truck's driver, Indian national Rajinder Kumar, was charged following the crash and has pleaded not guilty. Federal immigration authorities who later took him into custody say Kumar entered the U.S. illegally near Lukeville, Arizona, in November 2022 and was released by the Biden administration, pending immigration proceedings.

He later received work authorization and a CDL issued in California, according to Houston's FOX 26.

"If it weren't for that, our son and daughter-in-law would still be alive," Carter said, pinning blame on both federal and state policies that made the tragedy possible.

The heartbroken mother's comments came after speaking on Capitol Hill on Tuesday, when she pleaded for lawmakers to make changes to immigration policies.

ICE LAUNCHES CDL FRAUD TIPLINE AS DHS HIGHLIGHTS DEADLY CRASHES INVOLVING ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS

"[My son and daughter-in-law] lost the Russian roulette game our government is forcing them to play," she said.

"We allowed 10 million people in under Biden. How is there a different suggestion as to how to process them other than the same way they came into the country, en masse, leaving?"

"I have to say, as a lifelong Democrat, I am ashamed of what my party is doing."

Carter's husband, Dennis, also voiced frustration Thursday, focusing his criticism on policies that allowed Kumar to obtain a CDL.

"Just because someone is incompetent and can't do the job that they wanted to do, just because they got here, that doesn't mean, ‘Okay, they're here, we should give them a job that they can't do and just turn them loose on the road,’" he told "Hannity."

Dennis identified himself as a lifelong Republican and also offered a contrast to his wife's political background, saying their marriage demonstrates that political differences do not have to become personal divisions.

"We have learned that the two parties can exist in the same household, and we actually get along," he said.

Elizabeth agreed, saying the couple knows "how to disagree without tearing each other apart" and instead tries to better understand the issues on which they differ.

Elizabeth also imparted a challenge to the Democratic Party during her appearance, pleading for them to "grow up" and start communicating with ICE at the state level.

item.content:encoded:

I’m excited to see what happens tonight, as there is a Friday game between two top teams as Houston takes on Texas Tech.

IF YOU'RE LOOKING FOR A BIG 12 WINNER NOT NAMED TEXAS TECH OR BYU, CONSIDER THE HOUSTON COUGARS

TEXAS TECH HEAD COACH BLASTS USC, LINCOLN RILEY, FOR POOR ATTENDANCE AT LA COLISEUM IN WEEK ZERO

In the Oregon State games, Houston scored 33 and allowed 20. Texas Tech scored 35 and allowed 24 points. This puts both of those totals at 53 and 59. I am looking at the games and how they’ve been played and think the offenses are a bit ahead of the defenses for both squads. I like both quarterbacks in this game. I also think the running games should find their way to make an impact. Give me the over 53.5 for this one.

item.title: 'Scream' star admits he's 'ashamed' of sequel return after actress fired over anti-Israel comments
item.description: Matthew Lillard says he feels "ashamed" for returning to "Scream 7" after Melissa Barrera's firing, calling himself on the "wrong side of history."
item.content:encoded:
"Scream" actor Matthew Lillard said Tuesday that he felt "ashamed" for returning to the horror franchise after actress Melissa Barrera was fired over social media posts about Israel and the war in Gaza, telling fans during a 30th anniversary screening in Austin, Texas, that he believed he ended up on the "wrong side of history."

Lillard, who reprised his role as Stu Macher in the seventh installment, said his excitement about returning to the franchise overshadowed his concerns about how Barrera had been treated.

As reported by Entertainment Weekly, Lillard said, "I went back to do ‘Scream,’ and I got called out. And I’m like, ‘Oh, f---. That’s brutal.’" "I feel bad about that. I feel ashamed about that. Because in that moment I was so excited to go back, I didn’t really think about Melissa and that journey."

"I’m embarrassed, that’s the truth… I blew that. I’m on the wrong side of history for that. I still like being in the movie [but] it may not have been the best idea," Lillard continued.

PEREZ HILTON JOINS 'TOMI LAHREN IS FEARLESS' AND DECLARES CANCEL CULTURE IS NOW A SPORT

Barrera was dropped from the franchise in November 2023 after publishing and sharing a series of posts criticizing Israel following Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack.

In one post previously reported by Fox News Digital, Barrera accused Israel of committing "genocide" and "ethnic cleansing" in Gaza.

"Gaza is currently being treated like a concentration camp," Barrera said. "Cornering everyone together, with no where to go, no electricity no water … People have [learned] nothing from our histories. And just like our histories, people are still silently watching it all happen. THIS IS GENOCIDE & ETHNIC CLEANSING."

In another post, Barrera claimed Western news outlets were disproportionately presenting Israel's side of the conflict and told followers to draw their own conclusions about why.

‘NO JEWS, NO NEWS’ STRIKES AGAIN AS SELECTIVE COVERAGE OF THE 'UNSETTLERS' FUELS ANTI-ISRAEL ANGER

"Because western media only shows the other side. Why they do that, I will let you deduce for yourself," Barrera said.

Spyglass denied at the time that Barrera was removed merely for supporting Palestinians, instead saying it viewed some of her rhetoric as antisemitic.

"Spyglass’ stance is unequivocally clear: We have zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech," the company said.

Fox News Digital reached out to Spyglass Media for comment about Lillard's remarks.

Barrera subsequently rejected the suggestion that she was promoting antisemitism and defended her criticism of governments, Fox News Digital reported in May.

MORE THAN 180 JEWISH ENTERTAINERS RALLY BEHIND ACTOR MARK RUFFALO IN PROTEST LETTER

"I believe a group of people are not their leadership and that no governing body should be above criticism. I pray day and night for no more deaths, for no more violence and for peaceful co-existence," Barrera said.

The controversy resurfaced earlier this year when Barrera criticized former cast-mates who returned to the franchise without her. When asked whether actors who went back for "Scream 7" were "scabby," Barrera agreed.

"One hundred percent. I think they all are," Barrera said. "And they have to live with that."

At Tuesday’s screening, Lillard directly defended Barrera’s position and criticized the lack of public support she received after her firing.

"Melissa Barrera, who’s a beautiful actor, was fired for what she said after the whole Palestinian... what started happening in Israel," Lillard said. "It’s really f---ing bulls--- and really hard, and she’s on the right side of history."

"When that happened to Melissa, the whole world didn’t pipe up, but she was a year early on what the f---’s going on. But the whole world should have popped up and said, ‘She’s right.’ And they didn’t. And that’s brutal."

Despite the upheaval surrounding its development, "Scream 7" was released Feb. 27 and eventually crossed $200 million at the global box office, becoming the highest-grossing film in the franchise’s history, according to Paramount. The film shifted its focus back to Neve Campbell’s Sidney Prescott and brought back several franchise veterans, including Lillard.

When reached for comment by Fox News Digital, Hollywood in Toto editor Christian Toto said of Lillard’s remarks: "Now that the Palestinian cause is spiking in his far-Left industry, he has regrets. Now. Months after shooting the film. Months after its release. Months after the actress in question lost the role." 

Toto added, "Will he give all the money back? Does he know what she actually said about Israel and the timing of those comments? Is he aware of other artists who have had their free speech rights trampled?"

item.title: Roger Goodell details NFL expansion possibilities and a timetable for a full season of international games
item.description: Roger Goodell says Europe is the most likely home for NFL international expansion, envisioning two new franchise teams outside the United States.
item.content:encoded:
Commissioner Roger Goodell made the rounds during the NFL's first week of the regular season and into Thursday night's opening of the new Highmark Stadium in Buffalo. Out of that travel that spanned continents, we're getting a picture of his plans for league expansion.

Bottom line: Goodell sees NFL expansion outside the United States on the horizon.

"I think if we continue to grow, continue to get the kind of reaction, I do think a franchise will be international at some point in time," Goodell said prior to the Thursday night game between the Buffalo Bills and Detroit Lions on Prime's pregame show.

"I think Europe is the most likely [place], for a lot of reasons. One, the length of time we've been playing there. But also, the scheduling is going to be a lot easier."

ROGER GOODELL DISMISSES 49ERS COACH'S CONCERNS ABOUT PLAYING IN AUSTRALIA, SAYS IT'S PART OF LONG-TERM PLAN

The NFL began playing regular-season games in Europe in 2007 and to date has played 55 regular-season games there.

One could also argue Europe makes sense for international expansion because most of the teams in the AFC East and NFC East and some teams in the AFC South and NFC South are within a seven-hour flight to, say, London.

Other places simply don't make similar sense at this time.

"Australia might create a few complications for us," Goodell admitted.

NFL TO COMMEMORATE 25TH ANNIVERSARY OF 9/11 TERRORIST ATTACKS ACROSS ALL ITS STADIUMS AND EVEN IN AUSTRALIA

Goodell apparently is not thinking about expanding by one team in Europe. That would throw off the league's 32-team symmetry.

"I also believe we could have more than one team, which I think, ultimately, the support is there," Goodell said. "Two more teams."

So when will all this happen?

Goodell recently signed a new contract that carries his tenure as commissioner through the 2030 season. There has been speculation his goal is to have international expansion by the time his contract expires.

Is that the timeline?

"I don't think so," Goodell said on the Netflix pregame show recently. "There was no connection to the two.

"You know, listen, our vision here is to make it a global sport. The NFL deserves to be, it's a great game, and we all believe in it passionately."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

But while expansion by the end of the contract isn't a Goodell goal, having a full season's worth of international games is definitely on his radar.

This year the NFL is playing nine games abroad. Next year that number rises to a record 10 international games.

"I think our work here will be to get to 16 regular-season [International] games," Goodell said. "When we get to that point, then we'll be looking for the next, you know, stage to grow. But we think we'll be there in a few years.

"That may happen within four years."

item.title: GOP lawmakers smell something else behind Big Tech's AI doomsday warnings: 'Something else going on'
item.description: Capitol Hill lawmakers question whether OpenAI and Anthropic are pushing for AI regulation to stifle competition and lock in market dominance.
item.content:encoded:
Republicans on Capitol Hill are grappling over whether and how to regulate artificial intelligence companies even as top AI business leaders warn the technology could pose an existential threat to humanity.

The simmering debate over AI guardrails has exploded this week as House lawmakers worked through their final week in Washington until after the midterm elections. The flurry of activity was partially spurred by tech CEOs like Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman warning that the pace of innovation should be slowed after both companies saw AI models hack into other organizations of their own accord.

And while some in Congress are demanding swift action, others who spoke with Fox News Digital are questioning the motivation of AI companies in calling for the government to step in.

"I think there's a false sense of urgency," Rep. Troy Downing, R-Mont., told Fox News Digital.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS MEETS AI AS FEARS OF HUMAN EXTINCTION JOLT CAPITOL HILL

Downing spent his young adulthood in tech, having previously been a research scientist at the Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences at New York University and founding online calendar company WebCal, which was later acquired by Yahoo!.

"Yes, we should be taking it seriously, but I think the hyperbole is misplaced right now," Downing said. "Any one of those people crying gloom and doom has the possibility of stopping it in their own shops, so there's something else going on there."

Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., a former assistant U.S. attorney, also doubted AI companies' motives.

AI 'DOOMERS' RISK KNEECAPPING US VS CHINA, BUT EX-PENTAGON VET SAYS BOTH EXTREMES MISS THE MARK

"I'm very skeptical of people in big business who want to leverage big government to suppress competition," Knott said. "I'm afraid that's what we're seeing. That'd be like ... Google, Yahoo, Microsoft, Apple saying, 'We need to regulate all tech.' Whether it's software or hardware. It's like, guys, you're here already, right? And if there's one thing that I'm confident in, to protect AI for good, there has to be more than one option."

Still others believe lawmakers do not broadly have enough knowledge to take on AI guardrails.

Rep. Jimmy Patronis, R-Fla., told Fox News Digital that Congress should instead repeal Section 230, a federal law shielding internet and tech companies from liability for what third parties post.

"I think the warning is real, and I think that AI is unbelievable — look, AI is going to cure cancer. AI is going to find solutions to get rid of diseases that we never thought we could get rid of, but it does need to have some oversight. It needs a kill switch," Patronis conceded. "But again, I don't think Congress has the expertise to tell an emerging technology what's the best way to go."

Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., said when asked if Congress should act before the end of this year, "It's too complex a subject. You've got to understand it."

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump also joined the debate by dismissing AI companies' calls for more government regulation.

TRUMP UNLOADS ON TECH TITANS PUSHING FOR SLOWDOWN ON EMERGING INDUSTRY: ‘WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!’

"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX," he wrote on Truth Social. "The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"

But others are pushing for the government to step in to at least some degree, with some Republicans arguing for human guardrails to ensure AI does not go too far by itself.

RAND PAUL CLASHES WITH FELLOW REPUBLICAN OVER AI 'KILL SWITCH' AS SENATE GRAPPLES WITH 'TERMINATOR' FEARS

"The sooner we can act, the better," Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., chair of the House's AI task force, told reporters Wednesday. "Certainly, we've had some warning shots lately that have been very concerning ... So, God forbid we have a Chernobyl moment at some point here that really causes harm to people and focuses the public's attention on AI in a way that we hope it will never be."

When asked by Fox News Digital about Trump's warning, however, he said, "I think the president was talking about the dangers of over-regulation, and that's something I very much agree with him on."

RESEARCHER WHO DEPARTED AI ROLE OVER FEARS OF RACING INTO EXTINCTION SAYS PEOPLE ARE 'BEGGING' FOR REGULATION

Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., held a press conference alongside Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., on Thursday pushing legislation to stop "rogue" AI agents such as those that broke out of containment during trials by OpenAI and Anthropic.

"We want to make sure that people remain in control. This isn't about stopping AI or stifling innovation," Lawler said. "Some states have put a moratorium on the infrastructure that powers this technology. That does not invent a kill switch."

Gottheimer said the bill "tells the National Institute of Standards and Technology [to] get in a room and set standards, so organizations can find every agent on their network, verify who built it, who's running it, watch it in real time for anything suspicious, and cut off its access the second something looks wrong."
